Your House Hunting Scorecard

Compare up to eight homes on what actually matters to you.

Getting started

  1. Open House-Hunting-Scorecard.xlsx in Microsoft Excel on a desktop computer.
  2. If Excel opens it in Protected View, choose Enable Editing so the calculations run.
  3. Save your own copy and work in that.
  4. On Criteria, weight what matters to you from 1 to 5. Change the criteria themselves if yours are different.
  5. On Homes, add each place you see and score it 1 to 5 on every criterion.
Score each home the day you see it. By the seventh viewing they blur together, and a score written in the car is worth more than one reconstructed a week later.

The five tabs

  • Criteria — what matters to you, and how much.
  • Homes — one row per place, scored against every criterion.
  • Costs — what each one costs you every month.
  • Results — every home side by side, with cost per point.
  • Reference — every term and every assumption.

Before you start

Weights are the whole point. If commute is a 5 and parking is a 2, a home that wins on parking will not beat one that wins on commute. Set the weights honestly before you see anything, while you can still be objective.
Cost per point is the number to watch. It divides what a home costs each month by how well it scores. The cheapest home is not always the best value, and the highest scoring one rarely is.
This does not value a property or estimate a mortgage. Enter the monthly payment your lender quoted. A spreadsheet guess would be worse than the real number.

Cell colors

  • Cream cells — enter your own numbers here.
  • Gray cells — calculated automatically. Do not type in these.
  • Blue cells — editable assumptions.
